analogy.p: Imagine a reporter who watches only 10 minutes of a match and then writes a report on who played well. The score and key moments are the evidence for the conclusion. The evaluation is the reporter admitting that they watched only part of the game, that they stood behind a pillar, and that they would watch the whole match and use replays next time. This maps well onto sample size, limitations and improvements. It breaks down because a reporter can simply rewatch the game, whereas fieldwork conditions (such as river discharge on one particular day) cannot be repeated exactly.
analogy.t: A fieldwork enquiry is like a football match report

bullets: You must **draw conclusions** that answer the enquiry question or **support or reject** the hypothesis.
You must **link conclusions to the geographical theory or context** (for example the Bradshaw model, the Burgess model, distance decay or the bi-polar scale).
You must **evaluate the data collection methods**, including the sampling method and sample size.
You must **evaluate the presentation and analysis** techniques you chose.
You must comment on **reliability, validity, accuracy, limitations and sources of error**.
You must **suggest improvements** and say how they would improve the enquiry.
You must be able to do all of this for **unfamiliar fieldwork** as well as your own.
core.p: Under the fieldwork part of the AQA specification you must be able to **draw conclusions** from your fieldwork data and **evaluate** the enquiry. A conclusion is a reasoned answer to your enquiry question or hypothesis, supported by evidence from your own results. An evaluation is a judgement about how good the enquiry was: how far the methods gave data you can trust, how far the conclusion is supported, and how the investigation could be made better. In Paper 3 Section B you meet this both for your own two enquiries (one human, one physical) and for an unfamiliar enquiry described in the paper.

bullets: **Enquiry question**: the focus, e.g. 'How does pedestrian flow change with distance from the CBD?'
**Hypothesis**: a testable prediction, e.g. 'Pedestrian counts decrease as distance from the CBD increases.'
**Conclusion**: answers the question and states whether the hypothesis was **supported, partly supported or not supported**.
**Evaluation**: looks at the quality of methods, data, presentation, analysis and conclusion.
A flaw early on (such as too few sites) **weakens every later stage**, so always explain the knock-on effect.
The conclusion must use **your results**; the evaluation must use **the quality of the process**.
core.h: Where conclusion and evaluation fit in the enquiry process
core.p: A geographical enquiry follows a logical sequence: question or hypothesis, choice of methods, data collection, presentation, analysis, conclusion and finally evaluation. The conclusion looks back at the question and answers it, using the analysis. The evaluation then steps back from the whole process and judges it. Because the stages build on each other, a weakness at an early stage (for example a biased sampling method) reduces the reliability of everything that follows, and you should be able to explain that chain of cause and effect.

bullets: Start by answering the question directly: 'The hypothesis was **partly supported**...'
Back it up with **figures**: 'counts fell from 142 at the CBD to 25 at 600 m'.
Describe the **overall pattern** first, then **anomalies** (results that do not fit the trend).
Use a **statistic** if you calculated one: mean, median, range or interquartile range.
Explain the pattern using **geographical reasoning**: e.g. land values and accessibility fall with distance from the CBD.
Say how the results compare to the **expected model or theory**, and whether they match.
Use cautious language such as **'suggests'** and **'there is a general trend'** rather than 'proves'.
core.h: How to draw a valid conclusion
core.p: A good conclusion has three parts: it states the **overall answer** to the enquiry question, it supports this with **specific evidence from the data** (quoting figures, trends or statistics), and it **explains why** using geographical ideas. Examiners reward conclusions that refer to the actual data, mention anomalies honestly and avoid claiming more than the evidence shows. You should always be able to say how far the results agree with the theory you were testing.

bullets: **Supported**: most data points follow the predicted trend and anomalies are few.
**Partly supported**: the general trend is as predicted but with anomalies or a weak relationship.
**Not supported**: no clear pattern, or the pattern is the reverse of the prediction.
Always give **evidence** for your judgement (numbers, percentage of sites that fit).
Consider whether the **sample was large enough** to make the judgement safe.
A hypothesis can never be **proved** from limited data; it can only be supported by the evidence you collected.
core.h: Supported, partly supported or rejected hypotheses
core.p: Fieldwork rarely gives perfect results. A hypothesis is **supported** if the data clearly follow the predicted pattern, **partly supported** if the general trend matches but there are important anomalies or the pattern holds only for part of the data, and **not supported** if the data show no pattern or the opposite. Mark schemes reward you for justifying the level of support with evidence, so a clear 'partly supported' backed by figures scores better than an unsupported 'yes'.

bullets: Identify anomalies from **graphs** (points far from the line of best fit) or from **tables**.
Quote the anomalous value and **compare** it with the expected value.
Suggest a **local geographical reason** (e.g. a bus stop, a new development, a river confluence, a sheltered site).
Suggest a **possible error** (miscount, equipment fault, different time of day, weather).
Say whether the anomaly **changes the overall conclusion** (usually it does not, but it lowers confidence).
Suggest **repeating** that site to check if it is genuine.
core.h: Anomalies and how to treat them
core.p: An **anomaly** is a result that does not fit the general pattern. Good geographers do not hide anomalies; they identify them, suggest reasons and consider whether they are real or the result of error. For example, a site 400 m from the CBD with more pedestrians than a site at 300 m could be real (a bus stop or school nearby) or an error (counting at a busy time). Explaining anomalies shows understanding of both the place and the method.

bullets: **Rivers**: width, depth, velocity and discharge generally increase downstream; bedload becomes smaller and more rounded.
Explain with **processes**: attrition reduces bedload size, more tributaries add discharge, less friction in larger channels increases velocity.
**Coasts**: conclusions may describe beach profile, longshore drift or the effectiveness of coastal management.
Compare to the **Bradshaw model** or a similar model and say where data matched and where they differed.
Mention **local factors** (geology, tributaries, human structures) that caused anomalies.
State how confident you are, given the **sample size and the time of year**.
core.p: In physical enquiries (for example river or coastal fieldwork) conclusions usually describe how a variable changes downstream or along a coast and explain it using physical processes. For a river, you might conclude that width, depth and discharge increase downstream while bedload size decreases, and explain this using erosion, attrition, and increasing tributary input. The same structure applies: pattern, evidence, explanation, comparison with the Bradshaw model, and then anomalies such as a rock outcrop or a tributary inflow.

bullets: **Urban**: pedestrian flow, land values and building height tend to decrease away from the CBD; environmental quality may increase.
Link to **models**: Burgess (concentric rings), Hoyt (sectors) and bid-rent theory.
**Questionnaires**: describe percentages for each answer and note whether the sample was representative.
**Regeneration or change**: judge how far the area has improved using evidence such as new businesses, quality scores and opinions.
Mention **different groups** (residents, businesses, visitors) who may hold different views.
Comment on whether the **data are quantitative** (counts) or **qualitative** (opinions) and how that affects confidence.
core.p: In human enquiries (for example urban change, quality of life or regeneration) conclusions usually describe how a variable such as environmental quality, pedestrian flow or building height varies with distance from a centre or between areas, and explain it using theory such as the Burgess concentric zone model, bid-rent theory or the principle of accessibility. Because human fieldwork often uses questionnaires or scores, the conclusion should also acknowledge that people's opinions are subjective and may be influenced by the sample.

bullets: **Accuracy**: how close a measurement is to the true value (e.g. a ruler held at an angle across a river gives an inaccurate width).
**Reliability**: whether repeating the method gives similar results (e.g. repeating pedestrian counts at different times).
**Validity**: whether the method actually measures what the enquiry question asks about (e.g. a five-minute count at lunchtime may not represent a 'typical' day).
**Sample size**: too few sites or too few respondents makes results less representative.
**Sampling method**: random, systematic or stratified (see sampling) can introduce **bias** if poorly chosen.
**Equipment**: instrument error (e.g. flow meter blocked by weed) or limited precision (measuring to the nearest cm).
**Human error and bias**: subjective scoring, counting mistakes, leading questions in questionnaires.
core.p: When evaluating methods you judge whether the techniques you used gave data that were **accurate**, **reliable** and **valid**, and whether the sample was large and well chosen enough. Each method has typical strengths and weaknesses, and top answers refer to the specific method used (for example measuring width with a tape or counting pedestrians for five minutes) rather than giving generic points like 'human error'. You should state the weakness, the **effect on the results**, and an **improvement**.

bullets: **Accuracy**: correctness of the measurement compared with the real value.
**Reliability**: consistency of results if the method is repeated.
**Validity**: whether the data measure what the enquiry set out to investigate.
**Limitation**: a restriction on how far results can be trusted (small sample, one day only, weather).
**Source of error**: something that causes the data to differ from the true value (equipment, human error, timing).
Reliability is improved by **repeating** and taking **means**; validity is improved by choosing **appropriate methods** and **representative sampling**.
Accuracy is improved by better equipment, clearer procedures and **training** observers.
core.h: Reliability, validity, accuracy and limitations explained
core.p: These four words are often confused, and mark schemes reward correct, specific use. **Accuracy** is about being close to the true value. **Reliability** is about repeatability: do you get similar results if the data collection is repeated? **Validity** is about whether the data and method actually answer the question. A **limitation** is any weakness in the enquiry that restricts how far the results can be trusted or generalised. You can have reliable data that are not accurate (a consistently faulty instrument), as shown by the target figure.

bullets: **Time**: data collected on one day or at one time of day may not be typical (rush hour vs mid-morning; summer vs winter).
**Weather**: heavy rain changes river discharge; strong winds affect wave measurements; cold weather reduces pedestrian numbers.
**Equipment**: limited precision; faulty or poorly calibrated equipment; clinometer or tape misread.
**Human error**: inconsistent counting, poor technique, tired students, different people taking measurements.
**Subjectivity**: environmental quality scores or opinions vary between observers.
**Sample size**: small samples increase the effect of anomalies.
**Access and safety**: some sites could not be reached or were unsafe, so the pattern may be incomplete.
**Secondary data**: may be out of date or collected for a different purpose.
core.h: Common sources of error and limitation in fieldwork
core.p: You need a stock of precise sources of error that you can apply to any fieldwork context. Strong answers link each source of error to its effect on the data. For example 'the river was in spate after heavy rain, so velocity readings were higher than normal and the results are not representative of typical conditions'. The same data could be affected by time, weather, equipment, people or place.

bullets: **Random sampling**: each site or person has an equal chance; reduces bias but may leave gaps.
**Systematic sampling**: regular intervals (e.g. every 100 m); even coverage and easy to organise, but may miss variation between intervals.
**Stratified sampling**: sample proportions match the population (e.g. age groups); more representative but needs prior knowledge.
**Sample size**: bigger samples reduce the effect of anomalies, but take more time.
**Convenience sampling** (picking easy sites or friendly respondents) is likely to be **biased**.
Improvement: **increase sample size**, use a more appropriate method or sample at more sites.
core.p: Sampling is choosing a manageable number of sites or people from a larger population. **Random** sampling avoids bias but may miss important areas. **Systematic** sampling (every nth site or person) gives even coverage but can match a hidden pattern. **Stratified** sampling makes sure each sub-group is represented in proportion, but needs information about the population. Evaluation questions often ask whether your sampling was suitable and how it might create bias, so you should link the sampling technique to the data it produced.

bullets: Ask: did the technique **show the pattern clearly**? Did it suit the **type of data**?
**Strengths** of a scatter graph: shows correlation and anomalies; **weakness**: needs enough points.
**Strengths** of GIS maps and choropleths: show spatial patterns; **weakness**: can hide variation inside areas.
**Statistics** (mean, median, range, IQR) give a summary; the **mean** can be distorted by anomalies.
A line of best fit is a **judgement by eye**, so different students may draw different lines.
Improvement: use a **second technique** (e.g. add a table or map) to show the data in more than one way.
core.p: You must also judge whether the graphs, maps and statistics you used were the best choices. A technique is effective if it shows the pattern clearly, matches the data type and helps answer the question. It is less effective if it hides detail, is hard to read, or implies more precision than the data allow. For example, a bar chart may show differences between sites but not a relationship, while a scatter graph with a line of best fit shows correlation more clearly. Analysis is judged on how well it uses measures such as the mean, range and interquartile range to compare data.

bullets: Use the pattern: **'Do X, because it would Y.'**
**More sites or repeats** reduce the effect of anomalies and increase reliability.
**Collect at different times or days** to make results more representative.
**Better equipment** (e.g. a flow meter instead of an orange and stopwatch) increases accuracy.
**Clearer criteria** (e.g. agree what each score on an environmental quality survey means) reduces subjectivity.
**Larger or better-targeted sample** for questionnaires improves representativeness.
Extend the enquiry: **collect more data** in other places or **follow up with interviews** to explain patterns.
Combine your data with **secondary data** for comparison.
core.p: Improvements must be **specific, realistic and linked to a problem**. Examiners do not credit vague statements such as 'collect more data' or 'be more careful' without explanation. A strong improvement names exactly what would change, and explains how it would make the results more reliable, accurate or valid. For example: 'repeat the pedestrian counts on three different days and take a mean, which reduces the effect of unusual conditions on one day and makes the results more reliable'.

bullets: **Underline clues** in the stimulus: sample size, dates, weather, methods, equipment.
Use **command words**: assess, evaluate, suggest, to what extent, justify.
Quote **data** from the table or graph in conclusions.
Link each weakness to a **specific effect** on the results of the unfamiliar enquiry.
Make **different** improvement suggestions that fit this context, not a list copied from your own fieldwork.
For 'to what extent', give a **balanced judgement**: how far the evidence supports the conclusion, and what limits it.
core.p: In the exam, Section B also gives you a fieldwork scenario you have not seen: data tables, graphs, maps, or a description of how the data were collected. You apply exactly the same skills. Read the stimulus carefully for clues such as how many sites, what time of day, what equipment, what weather, and how the sample was chosen, then use those clues to comment on reliability and validity. Do not just use your own fieldwork; always refer to the information in the unfamiliar scenario.

bullets: Link to **enquiry questions and methods**: the quality of the question and methods decide how valid the conclusions are.
Link to **presentation and analysis**: the choice of graph and statistics supports (or weakens) the conclusion.
Link to **physical geography** (rivers, coasts) and **human geography** (urban change, development).
Link to **geographical skills**: calculate and interpret measures such as mean and IQR.
Link to **issue evaluation**: weigh evidence, recognise bias and make a reasoned judgement.
core.p: This sub-topic links directly to the other fieldwork and skills content. Conclusions rely on the data presentation and analysis skills, so you should be fluent in graphs and statistics. Evaluation builds on your knowledge of enquiry questions and methods, including risk assessment and sampling. It also links to topics tested elsewhere in the course: rivers, coasts, urban change and rural change provide the geographical theory that you use to explain fieldwork results. In Paper 3 Section A, the pre-release material asks for similar evaluative thinking about evidence.

exam: Command words: **'Suggest'** needs a reasoned idea; **'Assess'** and **'Evaluate'** need a judgement supported by evidence; **'To what extent'** needs a balanced conclusion.
1-mark questions often ask you to **state** a source of error or **identify** an anomaly from a graph.
2-mark questions: give **one point plus a development**, such as 'the sample was small, so an anomaly had a large effect'.
3 and 4-mark questions: give **two or three linked points** using the pattern problem, effect and improvement.
For 'suggest how the fieldwork could be improved', **name a specific change**, and explain **why** it would give more reliable or valid data.
For longer extended answers, structure the response as **conclusion, evidence, explanation, limitation, overall judgement**.
Always **quote data** from the question or your own results when you draw a conclusion.
Use precise words: **'reliable'** (repeatable), **'accurate'** (close to true value), **'valid'** (measures the right thing), **'representative'**.
On unfamiliar fieldwork, **highlight clues** (number of sites, dates, weather, equipment) and refer directly to them.
Do not just list limitations: **say how each limitation changes the conclusion** and give a realistic way to improve.
Plan the time: Section B is long, so aim for roughly **one mark per minute**.

mistakes.r: Say the hypothesis was supported, partly supported or not supported, because limited data cannot prove it.
mistakes.w: The results prove the hypothesis is correct.

mistakes.r: State the number of sites or repeats and explain how this reduces the effect of anomalies and improves reliability.
mistakes.w: Not enough data, so collect more data.

mistakes.r: Name the exact error (miscount, misread clinometer), explain how it affected the results, and say how to reduce it.
Identify the anomaly with a value, suggest a geographical reason or a possible error, and say how it affects confidence in the conclusion.
mistakes.w: The anomaly was a mistake and should be ignored.

mistakes.r: Reliability is consistency when repeated; accuracy is closeness to the true value.
mistakes.w: Reliability and accuracy are the same thing.

mistakes.r: The conclusion answers the question using data and geographical reasoning.
Quote at least two values or a statistic to support the pattern described.
mistakes.w: Conclusion with no figures from the data.

mistakes.r: Link the pattern to geographical theory or processes, such as Bradshaw model or distance decay.
mistakes.w: Only describing the pattern without explaining it.

mistakes.r: Use clues from the stimulus about sample size, timing, equipment and weather to write context-specific points.
mistakes.w: Copying evaluation points about their own fieldwork into an unfamiliar scenario.

summary: AQA GCSE Geography expects you to draw valid conclusions from your own fieldwork data, linked back to the original enquiry question and hypothesis, and then to evaluate the whole enquiry: the data collection methods, the sampling, the presentation and analysis, the reliability and validity of results, sources of error and limitations, and realistic improvements. These skills are tested on Paper 3 Section B for both your own fieldwork and unfamiliar fieldwork, so they matter for the longest-answer marks.

terms.d: A reasoned answer to the enquiry question or hypothesis, supported by evidence from the data.
A judgement about the quality of the enquiry, including methods, data, presentation, analysis and conclusions.
A testable statement or prediction that can be supported or rejected by data.
The question that focuses a geographical investigation.
A result that does not fit the general pattern of the data.
How close a measurement or result is to the true value.
The extent to which repeating the data collection would give similar results.
The extent to which the method and data measure what the enquiry set out to investigate.
A weakness in the enquiry that restricts how far the results can be trusted or generalised.
Anything that causes the recorded data to differ from the true value, such as equipment or human error.
Selecting a smaller number of sites or people to represent a larger whole.
The number of sites, measurements or respondents collected; larger samples are usually more reliable.
A systematic tendency in data collection or judgement that distorts the results.
Data collected first-hand by the student during fieldwork.
Data collected by someone else, such as census or Environment Agency data.
Numerical data that can be counted or measured.
Descriptive data about opinions or quality, such as interview responses.
Based on personal opinion or judgement and so likely to vary between people.
Typical of the whole population or situation being studied.

worked.ans: The hypothesis is largely supported. Counts decreased from 142 people at 0 m to 25 at 600 m, and six of the seven sites fit the trend. The 400 m site (71) is an anomaly because it is higher than the 300 m site (64), perhaps due to a bus stop nearby. With only seven sites, the anomaly lowers confidence slightly, but the overall conclusion still holds.
worked.q: Pedestrian counts at 7 sites between 0 and 600 m from the CBD were 142, 118, 96, 64, 71, 38 and 25. The hypothesis was that counts decrease with distance from the CBD. State whether the hypothesis is supported and justify your answer. (4 marks)
steps: Identify the pattern: the counts fall from 142 at 0 m to 25 at 600 m.
Count how many sites fit the trend: six of seven sites follow a decreasing trend.
Identify the anomaly: the 400 m site (71) is higher than the 300 m site (64).
Judgement: the general trend supports the hypothesis, but with one anomaly it is best described as largely supported.

worked.ans: The data are only moderately reliable. Counting for just five minutes on a single Tuesday lunchtime may not represent a typical day, and a short count near the busy CBD may be affected by miscounting. With only seven sites, one anomaly such as the 400 m site strongly affects the pattern. To improve reliability, repeat the counts at each site on several days and at different times of day and use the mean, so that unusual conditions have less influence and the conclusion is more valid.
worked.q: Evaluate the reliability of the data in the pedestrian count enquiry above, given that counts were taken for five minutes at each site on one Tuesday between 11 am and 1 pm. Suggest one improvement. (6 marks)
steps: Comment on time: one day and a short five-minute period are not necessarily typical, so the data may not be representative.
Comment on the effect: lunchtime may be busier near the CBD, so the pattern could be exaggerated.
Comment on sample: only seven sites means a single anomaly has a large effect.
Comment on human error: counters may miss pedestrians during busy periods.
Improvement: repeat counts at each site on several days and times and take a mean, which would reduce the effect of unusual conditions and improve reliability.
